overview: Between 1000 and 1783, Tibet developed influential monastic, artistic and medical traditions under changing regional rulers and relationships with Mongol and Qing powers. This atlas outline represents a broad plateau region, not one government continuously controlling every place inside it. It is distinct from the earlier Tibetan Empire and cannot establish later sovereignty.

periods.title: Monasteries and renewed learning
periods.summary: New religious networks grew across a politically divided region; Atisha arrived in central Tibet around 1042.

periods.title: Sakya and Mongol power
periods.summary: Sakya leaders became dominant with Mongol patronage and imperial authority behind them.

periods.title: Regional Tibetan rulers
periods.summary: Changchup Gyeltsen displaced Sakya hegemony in central Tibet; later internal conflicts weakened his Pakmodru successors.

periods.title: The Ganden Podrang government
periods.summary: The Fifth Dalai Lama and Mongol allies established a new government centered on Lhasa.

periods.title: Qing intervention and Tibetan institutions
periods.summary: Qing forces expelled the Dzungars; resident imperial representatives joined an evolving political order.

items.text: Around 1042, the Indian teacher Atisha arrived in central Tibet. Teaching journeys, new monasteries and exchanges of texts helped renew Buddhist learning. Monasteries became important economic and political institutions as well as places of worship, so an argument over religious leadership could also affect land and authority.

During the thirteenth century, Sakya leaders gained predominance through their relationship with Mongol rulers. Tibetan religious teachers also served at the Yuan court. This was a connection between religious influence and imperial power, rather than a single isolated mountain kingdom.

In 1354, Changchup Gyeltsen of Pakmodru took control of central Tibet and ended Sakya hegemony there. His successors later faced internal conflict. The following centuries therefore need several regional histories, rather than a straight list of rulers governing the entire plateau.

In 1642, the Fifth Dalai Lama and Mongol allies consolidated power after civil wars. The Ganden Podrang administration employed both monastic officials and secular nobles. Religious leadership and government were closely connected, but running the state also required offices, records and administrators.

Dzungar forces invaded in 1717; Qing and Tibetan forces drove them out in 1720. In 1727, Qing representatives called ambans became resident in Lhasa. Tibetan religious and political institutions continued within this changing relationship with the Qing empire.

The rulers of Gyantse sponsored an extraordinary monument: the Kumbum, built around 1427 to 1442 beside Pelkhor Chode monastery. Its regional patrons show that ambitious cultural projects flourished outside Lhasa. Political geography was a patchwork, and several towns could become important centers of learning and art.

Gyantse’s Kumbum contains 73 chapels and more than 20,000 images of deities. The arrangement follows an organized hierarchy of Buddhist teachings. Moving through the building was therefore also a journey through a religious curriculum: a library of painted rooms, with rather more stairs than a book.

Bon remained an active religious tradition. A fifteenth-century painting of its deity Trowo Tsochok Khagying survives on cloth with ink, color and gold. Organized Bon institutions developed during the tenth and eleventh centuries in interaction with Buddhism while drawing on older traditions. Tibet’s religious life was never only one school.

The Potala’s White Palace rose from 1645 to 1648; the Red Palace followed from 1690 to 1694. Thousands of artisans, engineers and conscripted laborers contributed. Its impressive walls also represent compulsory work, not simply the wishes or achievements of rulers.

Norbulingka began with the Uya Palace in 1751; the Gesang Palace followed in 1755 with a debate courtyard. It became the Dalai Lamas’ summer residence. The heritage account describes government departments moving there seasonally too: the paperwork had a summer address along with the ruler.

Medical students had spectacular revision aids. Desi Sanggye Gyatso commissioned 79 medical paintings from 1687 to 1697, alongside his commentary on the Four Tantras. Chakpori Medical College opened in 1696. Branching diagrams turned knowledge into memorable trees; many surviving illustrations are later copies of these designs.

The medical pictures include ordinary work: farmers and pastoralists milk animals, people prepare food together, and different water sources appear. Another painting shows fetal development and childbirth. These are unusually detailed windows into activities that grand portraits of rulers usually leave out.

Painting 64 illustrates examination of urine in bowls. Doctors also assessed the pulse and tongue. A patient’s pee could become a medical lesson! These images document historical diagnostic practices; they do not establish that every explanation or treatment was effective.

Anatomical disagreements could lead to investigation: the account of painting 49 describes examining human remains to settle questions about bones. The medical tradition included observation and debate alongside inherited texts. Even an authoritative book could prompt the question: does the body actually look like that?

Chokyi Dronma, born into a royal family in 1422, married and had a child before becoming a nun. She received full ordination, unusual for a Tibetan woman, and became the first figure in the Samding Dorje Pakmo incarnation line. Her story reveals a remarkable female religious leader with an earlier family life.

The young Lobzang Yeshe, recognized as a Panchen Lama, received a tutor for basic reading and writing after his enthronement at Tashilhunpo. His education then developed into years of religious study. This is evidence for one highly privileged child’s schooling, rather than a school timetable for every Tibetan household.

During the turmoil of the late 1720s, Lobzang Yeshe avoided face-to-face meetings because of the danger of smallpox, while continuing to communicate through messengers. The precaution shows disease affecting political and religious business. It was an attempt to reduce contact, centuries before email could rescue a cancelled meeting.

A surviving 1538 printing of Milarepa’s life was made at Ron Wosel Puk in Gungtang. Carving wooden printing blocks demanded skilled labor, paper and ink, but allowed multiple copies. It is the earliest surviving print of this biography, not the beginning of Tibetan printing.

Milarepa’s famous biography was composed by Tsangnyon Heruka in the late fifteenth century, long after the teacher’s lifetime. Its spiritual adventures helped make him widely known. The distance matters: a beloved religious life story is also literature, rather than a contemporary reporter’s transcript of every event.

A short Tibetan title is རྒྱུད་བཞི་, transliterated rgyud bzhi, meaning “Four Tantras.” The Grolier Club catalogue supplies this original-language title for a medical book dated around 1750, probably produced in Beijing. The witness shows Tibetan learning traveling beyond the plateau; the script here follows the catalogue’s transcription.

The same medical book’s cloth wrapper is called a na bza’, a “robe,” and its cord a ska rags, a “belt.” A book could be dressed with the vocabulary used for a monk’s clothing. The catalogue connects this careful treatment with reverence for the teacher and the teachings embodied in the text.

ending.text: The map stops in 1783, not at Tibet’s disappearance. Under changing political arrangements, the Ganden Podrang remained central Tibet’s government until 1959, when the Dalai Lama fled to India. Tibetan communities, language and religious traditions continued; neither this date nor the atlas polygon can settle modern sovereignty.
